reasoning: 1. TARGET ENGAGEMENT: Strong evidence of target engagement across all three targets. PD-L1 expression increased from baseline (1.7% at Cycle 1 Day 15, 2.7% at Cycle 3 Day 1) and CD8+ T cell infiltration increased (0.4% to 1.2%), confirming PD-1 checkpoint engagement. The BRAF/MEK pathway was also engaged as evidenced by the need for frequent dose modifications due to known on-target toxicities. 2. PATHWAY MODULATION: Downstream biology was successfully modulated. The increase in PD-L1 expression and CD8+ T cell infiltration demonstrates immune checkpoint pathway activation. The safety profile with frequent dose interruptions for dabrafenib (147/267 patients) and trametinib (238/267 patients) indicates MAPK pathway modulation. 3. CLINICAL TRANSLATION: Mixed clinical results. The primary endpoint (PFS) showed a trend toward benefit (HR 0.82, p=0.042) but did not meet the pre-specified significance threshold. However, there was clear clinical benefit in the PD-L1 positive subgroup (26.6 vs 15.4 months PFS). 4. POPULATION EFFECTS: Strong differential response by PD-L1 status. PD-L1 positive patients had substantial benefit (26.6 vs 15.4 months), while PD-L1 negative patients had modest benefit (12.0 vs 10.3 months). This suggests the mechanism works effectively in the biomarker-selected population. 5. CONFOUNDERS: Dose-limiting toxicities and frequent dose modifications may have limited efficacy in some patients, but the biomarker-driven response pattern suggests the primary issue was population selection rather than dosing.

failure_modes.evidence: Clear efficacy signal in PD-L1 positive subgroup (26.6 vs 15.4 months PFS) while PD-L1 negative patients showed minimal benefit (12.0 vs 10.3 months). The overall population result was driven down by inclusion of non-responding PD-L1 negative patients.
